source_text: Καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον λέγω, οὐκ ἀπιστῶν ὁ Χριστιανὸς τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ, ἀλλὰ δυσωπῶν ἐκ τῶν κοινῇ ἡμῖν πεπιστευμένων ὅτι πολλῷ οὗτος ἐκείνων ἄξιός ἐστι τοῦ πιστεύεσθαι τοιαῦτα λέγων ἑωρακέναι καὶ ὡς εἰκὸς παραδοὺς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἣν εἶδεν ὄψιν καὶ τὴν φωνὴν ἧς ἤκουσεν. ἄλλος δ᾿ ἄν τις εἴποι ὅτι οὐ πάντες τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἤκουσαν ταῦτα διηγουμένου οἱ ἀναγράψαντες τὰ περὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς καὶ τῆς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ φωνῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ διδάξαν Μωϋσέα πνεῦμα τὴν πρεσβυτέραν αὐτοῦ ἱστορίαν, ἀρξαμένην ἀπὸ τῆς κοσμογενείας μέχρι τῆς κατὰ τὸν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ, τοῦτ᾿ ἐδίδαξε καὶ τοὺς γράψαντας τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τὸ γενόμενον παράδοξον κατὰ τὸν χρόνον τοῦ βαπτίσματος Ἰησοῦ. ὁ δὲ κοσμηθεὶς χαρίσματι καλουμένῳ „λόγῳ σοφίας“ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν διηγήσεται τῆς ἀνοίξεως τῶν οὐρανῶν καὶ τοῦ εἴδους τῆς περιστερᾶς, καὶ ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλου τινὸς ζῴου εἴδει ἢ τούτου ἐφάνη τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τῷ Ἰησοῦ. περὶ τούτου δὲ οὐκ ἀπαιτεῖ νῦν ἡμᾶς ὁ λόγος διηγήσασθαι· τὸ γὰρ προκείμενόν ἐστιν ἐλέγξαι τὸν Κέλσον οὐχ ὑγιῶς Ἰουδαίῳ περιθέντα μετὰ τοιῶνδε λόγων ἀπιστίαν περὶ πράγματος, κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς γενομένου μᾶλλον παρὰ τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου.
pass_a_gloss: And I say these things to the Jew, the Christian not disbelieving Ezekiel and Isaiah, but having respect for them from the things which have been commonly entrusted to us, that this one is much more worthy of being believed than those when saying such things as he has seen and as is likely handing over to the disciples the vision which he saw and the voice which he heard. Another might say that not all of Jesus' disciples heard him narrating these things, those who wrote about the appearance of the dove and the voice from heaven; but the Spirit which taught Moses, the older history, which began from the creation of the world until the time of Abraham, his father, this also taught those who wrote the Gospel, the paradox which occurred at the time of Jesus' baptism. And the one who has been adorned with the charisma called 'word of wisdom' will also narrate the reason for the opening of the heavens and the appearance of the dove, and that the Holy Spirit appeared to Jesus not in the form of any other animal but in this form. But now the discussion does not require us to narrate this; for what is at issue is to refute Celsus, who has not rightly put on Jewishness with such words of unbelief about a matter, which has likely occurred more than what was believed by him.

pass_b_english: I address these words to the Jew. The Christian does not disbelieve Ezekiel or Isaiah; rather, out of respect for what has been entrusted to us in common, we hold that Christ is far more worthy of belief than they are when he says he has seen such things and, as is likely, handed on to his disciples the vision he saw and the voice he heard. (Ezekiel; Isaiah) Someone else might object that not all of Jesus' followers heard him recount these events — the writers who describe the dove's appearance and the voice from heaven. Yet the Spirit that taught Moses his earlier history, from the creation of the world down to the time of Abraham his father, is the same Spirit that taught the Gospel writers the paradoxical event that occurred at Jesus' baptism. And the one who has been graced with the gift called 'the word of wisdom' will also explain why the heavens opened and why the dove appeared, and why the Holy Spirit showed himself to Jesus in that form and not in the form of any other creature. The present discussion does not require us to go into that now; the point is to refute Celsus for falsely adopting a Jewish persona in order to express disbelief about an event that, by all likelihood, actually happened — contrary to what he chooses to believe.

review.notes: Pass A fails on agency and sense in the first sentence: 'this one is much more worthy of being believed than those when saying such things' (Pass A) misrepresents 'οὐτ ἄξιός ἐστι τοῦ πιστεύεσθαι τοιαῦτα λέγων' (this one is much more worthy of being believed [than those] when saying such things). The Greek structure implies the worthiness of Christ is linked to the truth of his claims, but Pass A's phrasing 'than those when saying' is syntactically broken and obscures the comparison. More critically, Pass A fails the 'agency' and 'doctrine' check regarding the final clause: 'which has likely occurred more than what was believed by him' (Pass A) is a poor rendering of 'κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς γενομένου μᾶλλον παρὰ τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου' (which, according to probability, happened more [in accordance with likelihood] than what he believed). Pass A suggests the occurrence was 'more' than the belief, whereas the Greek argues the event is more probable/likely than his belief allows. Pass B is superior, but Pass A's failure to maintain the sense of the comparison and the probability clause necessitates a fail.
reasons: Pass A: 'this one is much more worthy of being believed than those when saying such things' (Pass A) fails to accurately render the Greek comparison and syntax 'οὐτ ἄξιός ἐστι τοῦ πιστεύεσθαι τοιαῦτα λέγων' (this one is much more worthy of being believed [than those] when saying such things).

Pass A: 'which has likely occurred more than what was believed by him' (Pass A) fails to capture the probabilistic sense of 'κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς γενομένου μᾶλλον παρὰ τὰ πεπιστευμένα ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνου' (which, according to probability, happened more [in accordance with likelihood] than what he believed).
